title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text: Gilbert, J. B., Himmelsbach, Z., Miratrix, L. W., Ho, A. D., and Domingue, B. W. (2025). Item-level heterogeneity in value added models: Implications for reliability, cross-study comparability, and effect sizes. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics. doi

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Why This Paper Matters
Value-added models (VAMs) are often used to compare teacher or school effectiveness, but they usually treat test scores as if the specific items on a test do not matter for the estimated value-added effect. This paper shows that assumption can be too strong. When effects vary across items (cluster-by-item interactions), standard VAM specifications can overstate both reliability and between-cluster differences.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Core Question
How much bias is introduced when value-added models ignore item-level heterogeneity in cluster effects?

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Approach

Reframes VAM reliability through Generalizability Theory.
Derives analytic results for how omitted cluster-by-item variance biases reliability and variance estimates.
Validates analytic predictions through simulation across different sample sizes, item counts, and pretest reliabilities.
Applies methods empirically to 16 academic outcomes from 8 U.S. studies with item-level outcomes and baseline data.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Visual Snapshot 1: Why Misspecification Happens

The paper’s conceptual diagram shows that when cluster-by-item variance is omitted, that variance gets absorbed into other components, creating inflated estimates of reliability and cluster-effect dispersion.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Main Findings (Quantitative)
In the empirical sample (16 outcomes, 8 studies, 31,349 respondents, 617 items):

Standard VAMs overstated reliability by a median of 0.04 on the 0-1 scale (mean = 0.09, SD = 0.10).
Standard deviations of cluster effects were a median of 3% too large (mean = 12%, SD = 23 percentage points).
Cluster-by-item variance frequently accounted for more than 50% of total item-level VA variance in these datasets.

In simulation:

Bias in reliability was positive whenever cluster-by-item variance was omitted.
Bias generally increased as the proportion of cluster-by-item variance increased.
Correctly specified item-level models had lower reliability RMSE than misspecified constant-effect models.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
section: Visual Snapshot 2: Simulation Evidence of Reliability Bias
text:
Visual Snapshot 2: Simulation Evidence of Reliability Bias

Across many simulation settings, misspecified constant-effect models systematically show higher bias than item-level models that account for cluster-by-item interactions.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
section: Visual Snapshot 3: Empirical Magnitude of Item-Level Heterogeneity
text:
Visual Snapshot 3: Empirical Magnitude of Item-Level Heterogeneity

The empirical datasets show moderate-to-high proportions of value-added variance attributable to cluster-by-item interactions, consistent with the simulation and analytic argument that omission can distort reliability.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Interpretation for Research and Policy

Reliability estimates from standard VAMs should be treated as upper bounds when item-level heterogeneity is plausible and items vary across administrations.
Comparisons across studies/tests are harder than they appear because different item sets can change estimated value-added precision.
Effect-size interpretation is impacted: if reliability is overstated, downstream correlations and inferences can be mis-calibrated.
Risk is context-dependent: bias may be modest in long, stable, high-quality testing programs but can be meaningfully larger in shorter or changing assessments.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Practical Implications

If item-level data are available, estimate interaction-allowing item-level models (or sensitivity checks) alongside conventional VAMs.
Report both:

a conventional reliability estimate, and
an adjusted estimate accounting for cluster-by-item interactions.

In high-stakes decisions, explicitly communicate how much reliability depends on test-item composition.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Limits Noted by the Authors

Results are strongest for settings with item-level data and single-occasion reliability framing.
Magnitude of bias can vary with test design, item count, and whether items are reused across occasions.
Conclusions focus on reliability/measurement precision and do not solve broader identification concerns in VAM causal interpretation.

title: Draft Two-Page Brief: Item-Level Heterogeneity in Value-Added Models
text:
Bottom Line
This paper shows that item-level heterogeneity is not a technical nuisance; it is a consequential source of measurement error in value-added inference. Ignoring cluster-by-item interactions can inflate reliability and exaggerate differences between teachers or schools, with direct implications for policy use and comparative research.

title: Item-Level RCT Datasets
text: To support my interests in psychometrics and causal inference and to enhance research in this area generally, I have curated a collection of empirical item-level outcome data from RCTs. The datasets are publicly accessible in a harmonized format on the Item Response Warehouse (IRW). At present, the RCT datasets in the IRW span over 100 outcome measures across dozens of RCTs in education, psychology, economics, and health. The datasets all begin with the prefix gilbert_meta in the IRW for ease of access and analysis.

title: Item-Level RCT Datasets
text:
Derivative Research
These item-level datasets have supported research on:

item-level heterogeneous treatment effects,
sensitivity of value-added and average treatment effect estimates to measurement and preprocessing choices,
attenuation bias and outcome scaling,
socially desirable responding in intervention studies.
